title: Shifts and Reflections of Graphs
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Describe how adding constants to f(x) or to x shifts a graph vertically and horizontally, and how multiplying by -1 reflects it, illustrating with f(x) = x^2.
finalAnswer: $f(x)+c$ shifts up $c$, $f(x)+(-c)$ down; $f(x+c)$ shifts left $c$; $-f(x)$ reflects across the $x$-axis and $f(-x)$ reflects across the $y$-axis.

steps.title: Vertical Shifts Act on the Output
steps.explanation: Adding a constant to the whole formula raises or lowers every point of the graph by the same amount without changing its shape. Adding inside the output is the intuitive direction: plus means up.
steps.why: Output changes move the already-computed height, so their effect matches the sign.

steps.title: Horizontal Shifts Act on the Input and Feel Reversed
steps.explanation: In f(x + c) the vertex of y = x^2 moves to x = -c, so adding 3 inside shifts the parabola left by 3. The rule moves left because the input must now be 3 smaller to reach the same value the original function produced.
steps.why: Input changes must be undone before the function sees them, which reverses the apparent direction.

steps.title: Reflections Come from Negatives
steps.explanation: The graph of -f(x) mirrors y = f(x) across the x-axis, turning the upward parabola downward. The graph of f(-x) mirrors across the y-axis; for x^2 the mirror is invisible because the parabola is already y-axis symmetric, but for x^3 the flip is very visible.
steps.why: A negative outside the function flips vertically; a negative inside flips horizontally.

steps.title: Combine Rules in Order
steps.explanation: To graph g, start with x^2, shift right 2 (input rule), reflect over the x-axis (negative outside), then shift up 5 (output rule). The vertex lands at (2, 5) opening downward.
steps.why: Practising a multi-step combination shows that shifts and reflections compose like a recipe.
